what: Amentum provides engineering and technical services to governments. Its people manage nuclear sites, maintain military equipment and bases, run intelligence and cyber programmes, and provide engineering for space and energy projects. It was formed by combining Amentum with Jacobs’ government services business.
customers: The United States Department of Defense and intelligence agencies, the Department of Energy, NASA, and allied governments, under contracts lasting years.
money: Engineering, nuclear site management, space and environmental programmes.
Intelligence, cyber, systems engineering and mission support.
moat: Classified government work requires thousands of staff holding security clearances and facilities accredited to handle secret material, which takes years and cannot be bought quickly. Nuclear site management in particular is open to a very short list of qualified contractors, and the contracts run for decades.
risks: Debt of $4.2B against $437.0M of cash is heavy, a legacy of the merger that created the company.
Last year’s net margin was 0.5%, and reported net income of $204.0M on $14.1B of revenue is a 1.4% margin — government services is a thin-margin industry.
The merger more than doubled revenue in one step, which makes the financial history hard to read and integration risk real.
Government contract margins are capped by the contracting rules, so there is a ceiling on profitability.
Twelve analysts average a $29.25 target against a $21.02 price, a 39% gap.
opportunities: Free cash flow of $474.0M against a $5.1B market value is a 9.3% yield, and the shares trade at about 10.8 times free cash flow.
At 0.36 times sales and 8.5 times EV/EBITDA, the enterprise is priced modestly.
Security clearances and accredited facilities make the customer base effectively closed to new entrants.
Nuclear site management contracts run for decades and have a very short list of qualified bidders.
Revenue of $14.1B gives scale advantages in bidding and in overhead absorption.
watch: Backlog and contract win rate. Government services revenue is booked years ahead, so the order book describes the future while the income statement describes contracts won earlier.
view: Government services is a business of thin margins and high barriers, and both halves matter. The margins are thin by design: government contracting rules cap what a contractor may earn, so nobody in this industry gets rich per dollar of revenue. Amentum earns about 1.4% net on $14.1 billion. The barriers are high and real: thousands of staff with security clearances, facilities accredited to handle classified material, and a track record on programmes where failure is unacceptable. New entrants do not appear.

Within that, the best part of Amentum is nuclear site management. Cleaning up and operating American nuclear facilities is work that a handful of contractors are qualified to do, the contracts run for decades, and the funding is committed by statute rather than argued over annually. That is about as close to an annuity as government contracting gets.

The complication is the merger. Combining with Jacobs’ government services business more than doubled revenue in one step — from $8.4 billion to $14.4 billion — which makes the financial history nearly unreadable and leaves $4.2 billion of debt on the balance sheet. Integration of two large services organisations means merging clearance administration, overhead structures, contract vehicles and cultures, and it is where mergers of this type usually disappoint.

At 0.36 times sales, 8.5 times EV/EBITDA and 10.8 times free cash flow, the market is pricing integration risk and the debt rather than doubting the business. The twelve analysts at $29.25 are modelling the synergies arriving. What determines the answer is backlog and win rate — whether the combined company is winning the recompetes and new programmes that replace work as it finishes. The income statement here describes contracts won two or three years ago and tells you nothing about that.
bull: The merger’s cost synergies arrive while a clearance-protected franchise wins recompetes, and $474 million of free cash flow deleverages a 0.36 times sales business.
bear: Integration stumbles and recompetes are lost, thin government margins leave no cushion, and $4.2 billion of debt sits on a business earning 1.4% net.
